accuracy.evidence: The body changes match the sympathetic response described by Harvard Health and the APA: faster heart and breathing, tensed muscles, dilated pupils and slowed digestion, driven by adrenaline with cortisol from the HPA axis. Good stress is framed as short, manageable challenge with control, matching the eustress literature, and the two-week sign for persistent low mood and poor sleep follows NHS guidance. Exercise lowering adrenaline and cortisol and slow exhale-led breathing lowering heart rate both have published support.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs that all stress is harmful, that normal pre-test butterflies mean illness, that a short scare is worse than months of low-level stress, that coping is judged by how it feels in the moment (scrolling, energy drinks), that fast deep breaths calm you, and that weeks of stress should be handled alone.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics are specific to the stress response: a tap-the-body alarm map, three draggable size/length/control dials with a live good or bad verdict, a weekly stress-hormone line where recovery chips dropped into gaps bring each spike down, a tool-to-reason matcher, and a press-and-hold breathing pacer. None of this is the mood diary, stress bucket or service matcher used in the mental health lab (flagwell).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes one idea visible: the alarm map shows why butterflies happen, the dials show that the same football final can be good or bad stress depending on size, length and control, the week line shows why recovery matters more than any single spike, and the matcher answers the assessment prompt by tying each strategy to why it works.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions come before the action: whether digestion speeds up or slows when the alarm fires, whether all stress is bad, whether one big day or weeks of medium stress is worse, and which breathing pattern calms you. Each wrong option is a common belief the following task then corrects.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating situations (test nerves, long worry versus short scares, why running helps, three weeks of no sleep, swamped by deadlines, calming breaths) each give a specific reason for every wrong answer, such as energy drinks pushing the alarm up or avoidance letting pressure build.

readability.evidence: Learner paragraphs use short sentences and plain words for 11 to 12 year olds, with the two hormone names explained once. Canvas labels are short, the dial labels are everyday words such as Hours, Weeks and A little, and challenge feedback is one or two sentences.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a fact or a check: what the alarm does, the three tests for bad stress, why recovery matters, and the two-week sign. There are no greetings, scene-setting or praise padding in the text, prompts or lab copy.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 and a 360 px Android viewport in light and dark themes: body hotspots are large circles, dials drag across the full width with plus and minus buttons as a fallback, recovery chips wrap into two rows, and the breathing pacer works by holding the canvas or the button.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin, including the breathing button that responds to holding Space or Enter. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every change with the alarm state, dial values, gap contents, matches or breath count, and the axe scan is clean in both themes.
